title: Auditing black-box clinical prediction models with a large language model through queries alone: a blinded test with planted flaws
authors: Zhiyu Liu, Xinyu Yang
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are used to explain clinical prediction models, on the promise that they can say what a model computes, find its faults and even reveal new knowledge in it. We tested the three promises where the answers could be checked. From the International Stroke Trial we trained four kinds of model (logistic regression, explainable boosting machine, gradient-boosted trees, neural network) for two outcomes on patients randomised earlier, planted one flaw in each of 24 copies (an under-predicted subgroup, a reversed risk factor or an implausible step) and mixed them with the 8 clean models. GPT-6 Astra audited each model three times, blind, through a tool that only returned the model's predictions; the judging rules were committed before any run and applied by program. Its surrogate models, with a median of 128 terms, reproduced the audited models' log-odds with a mean $R^2$ of 0.976 (0.959 for an additive surrogate of 42 terms fitted by an analyst). It found the planted flaw in 69 of 72 runs (96%; 95% CI 80% to 99%); a script written for the purpose found all 24. It also reported many more problems: 60% of 1,089 checkable reports failed the pre-specified check against the model's average behaviour; post hoc, most of these were real but small steps, and 15% of the checkable reports were not found in the model. Of 601 unexpected relationships it read out of the clean models, 11% held in patients randomised later (random pairs 6%; a regression scan's shorter list of its strongest candidates, 28%); after a check on the training data, 33% against 30%. With query access alone, an LLM can describe a black-box model faithfully and find nearly every planted flaw, as a purpose-written script also did; its reports of problems must be checked on the model and its discoveries on data.

infographic.key_insight: A query-only LLM auditor closely reproduced clinical prediction models and detected 96% of planted flaws, but its additional warnings and discoveries required independent validation.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Black-box model audits can use LLM-generated probes and surrogate models, provided warnings are checked against model behavior and discoveries against held-out data.
method: Trained four model types on International Stroke Trial data for two clinical outcomes.
Mixed 24 models with planted flaws and 8 clean models; GPT-6 Astra audited each three times using prediction queries alone.
Scored audits programmatically with precommitted rules and tested unexpected relationships in later-randomized patients.
infographic.evidence_signal: Surrogates achieved mean log-odds R² of 0.976, and the auditor found 69/72 planted flaws across runs; a purpose-written script found all 24 distinct flaws.
infographic.watch_item: Beyond planted flaws, 60% of checkable problem reports failed the prespecified check, and only 11% of unexpected relationships held in later patients.
infographic.paper_title: Auditing black-box clinical prediction models with a large language model through queries alone: a blinded test with planted flaws

title: Atomic MathReasoner: Instance-Level Composition of Atomic Reasoning Skills for Mathematical LLMs
authors: Jiashu Li, Tianyu Gao, Qinglong Liu, Jinping Wang, Ye Wei, Zhiqiang Gao
abstract: Most existing approaches enhance mathematical reasoning in large language models (LLMs) as a monolithic capability, despite the fact that different mathematical problems require different reasoning skills. Recent work has explored a more fine-grained perspective by decomposing mathematical reasoning into atomic skills and developing specialized modules for individual capabilities. However, how to effectively utilize these atomic abilities remains underexplored. To address this challenge, we propose Atomic MathReasoner (AMR), an instance-level framework for composing atomic reasoning skills. AMR first trains a library of capability-specific LoRA experts and performs gradient-free optimization over held-out validation subsets to discover a diverse set of low-loss composition prototypes. It evaluates the preference of each prototype using the token-level negative log-likelihood of reference solutions, filters ambiguous assignments through a confidence margin, and distills the resulting pseudo-labels into a lightweight router. During inference, the router selects an appropriate composition prototype for each problem, enabling problem-specific utilization of atomic skills without costly online optimization. Experiments on the AtomicMath benchmark across general and mathematics-specialized LLMs demonstrate consistent improvements. On Qwen2.5-Math-Instruct-7B, AMR increases average field accuracy from 64.4% to 68.1% at Level 1 and from 59.3% to 63.7% at Level 2, while improving average logical reasoning performance from 39.4% to 46.8%. These results demonstrate that effectively composing specialized atomic skills provides a promising approach to strengthening mathematical reasoning in LLMs.

infographic.key_insight: Atomic MathReasoner improves mathematical reasoning by selecting a problem-specific composition of specialized atomic-skill experts.
infographic.engineering_relevance: A lightweight router selects precomputed LoRA compositions at inference, avoiding costly online composition optimization.
method: Train capability-specific LoRA experts and discover low-loss composition prototypes through gradient-free optimization on held-out validation subsets.
Score prototypes using reference-solution token-level negative log-likelihood and filter ambiguous assignments with a confidence margin.
Distill the resulting pseudo-labels into a router that selects a composition for each problem.
infographic.evidence_signal: On AtomicMath with Qwen2.5-Math-Instruct-7B, average field accuracy rose from 64.4% to 68.1% at Level 1 and 59.3% to 63.7% at Level 2; average logical reasoning performance rose from 39.4% to 46.8%.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract does not establish whether the learned compositions and router generalize beyond AtomicMath.
infographic.paper_title: Atomic MathReasoner: Instance-Level Composition of Atomic Reasoning Skills for Mathematical LLMs

title: Self-Rewarded Reinforcement Learning for Better-Structured Medical Explanations in Small Language Models
authors: Prakhar Mishra, Bhavya Yajush Awasthi, Tanuja, Nishant
abstract: Small language models (SLMs) can run on commodity hardware and support privacy-preserving, on-premises clinical deployment, but their medical explanations are often short and poorly structured compared with large language models. Recent supervised approaches such as Meerkat transfer chain-of-thought reasoning into 7B-8B backbones, yet their training objective does not directly target the style or organization of the generated rationales. Building on the instruction-tuned Mistral-7B backbone, we investigate whether a lightweight reinforcement learning (RL) step can improve explanation structure without human preference labels.We apply Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) with LoRA adaptation to 2,000 Meerkat-derived medical prompts, guided by a simple self-supervised reward that favors longer, lexically diverse, and well-punctuated responses while penalizing very short ones. Training for about 170 PPO steps on a single NVIDIA A100 GPU yields a stable increase in the average reward. Quantitative and qualitative comparisons show that the RL-tuned model produces longer, more organized, multi-point explanations while preserving the underlying medical content.We discuss the promise and the limitations of self-rewarded RL for shaping the style of medical explanations.

infographic.key_insight: Self-rewarded reinforcement learning improved the length and organization of Mistral-7B medical explanations without human preference labels.
infographic.engineering_relevance: PPO with LoRA offers a lightweight route to shaping explanation style in small models intended for on-premises clinical deployment.
method: Start with instruction-tuned Mistral-7B and 2,000 Meerkat-derived medical prompts.
Apply PPO with LoRA using rewards for length, lexical diversity, and punctuation, plus penalties for very short responses.
Train for about 170 PPO steps on one NVIDIA A100 GPU.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports rising average reward and quantitative and qualitative comparisons showing longer, more organized, multi-point explanations while preserving underlying medical content.
infographic.watch_item: Style-based rewards may favor verbosity without improving clinical correctness; the abstract does not establish clinical safety.
infographic.paper_title: Self-Rewarded Reinforcement Learning for Better-Structured Medical Explanations in Small Language Models

title: Thermodynamics of gas giants accreting via shocks: the role of molecular hydrogen dissociation
authors: Bingjie Zha, Zhuo Chen
abstract: Within the core-accretion framework, gas giants acquire most of their mass through accretion shocks during runaway gas accretion. The shock thermodynamics---governed by radiative cooling, accretion history, and equation of state (EoS)---sets the post-shock gas entropy and initial thermal state, strongly influencing both observables and subsequent evolution. We aim to build a coupled evolutionary model predicting the initial thermodynamic conditions, intrinsic luminosities, and upper limits on magnetic field strengths of gas giants across diverse accretion histories. We couple radiation hydrodynamics and $\mathrm{H_2}$ dissociation to long-term planetary interior evolution by training a physics-informed neural network (PINN) predictor on 1000 first-principles simulations resolving the shock physics. This PINN provides post-shock outer boundary conditions for MESA to evolve the planetary envelope beyond runaway accretion. The PINN predicts higher post-shock temperatures than the canonical cold-start model, with the discrepancy widening with planetary mass, while post-shock entropy jumps sharply when $\mathrm{H_2}$ dissociates at $\sim 2000$ K. Gas giants evolved with PINN-derived boundary conditions achieve intrinsic luminosities 4--10 times higher than cold-start models. Under optimistic assumptions, the maximum magnetic field strength at $2 R_{\mathrm{J}}$ reaches a few gauss for a $0.3 M_{\mathrm{J}}$ planet, $\sim 100$ G for $1 M_{\mathrm{J}}$, and $\sim 500$ G for $3 M_{\mathrm{J}}$. Incorporating detailed radiation hydrodynamics and realistic thermodynamics into accretion shock models yields higher initial entropies, brighter intrinsic luminosities, and stronger magnetic fields, providing improved constraints on the masses and accretion rates of directly imaged exoplanets.

infographic.key_insight: A physics-informed neural network linking accretion-shock physics to planetary evolution predicts hotter, higher-entropy gas giants with intrinsic luminosities 4–10 times those of cold-start models.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The coupled workflow connects detailed shock simulations to long-term planetary evolution, improving model-based interpretation of directly imaged exoplanets.
method: Train a physics-informed neural network on 1,000 first-principles accretion-shock simulations.
Include radiation hydrodynamics and molecular hydrogen dissociation.
Use predicted post-shock boundary conditions in MESA planetary-evolution calculations.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports a sharp post-shock entropy jump near hydrogen dissociation at approximately 2,000 K and evolved intrinsic luminosities 4–10 times higher than cold-start predictions.
infographic.watch_item: Magnetic-field estimates are optimistic upper limits, and the abstract provides no held-out prediction errors or observational validation.
infographic.paper_title: Thermodynamics of gas giants accreting via shocks: the role of molecular hydrogen dissociation

title: Depth Before Breadth: Reverse-to-Forward Curriculum with Advantage Decomposition for LLM Agent
authors: Siyuan Du, Yuxin Liu, Meng Tang, Haoran Li, Yechao Bai, Feiyang Pan
abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) has become a common approach for training large language model (LLM) agents on long-horizon tasks. However, learning from sparse terminal rewards makes credit assignment and exploration difficult. We approach these challenges through a policy-induced capability region, the set of states from which the current policy can reliably complete a task. Near its boundary, an agent may need only a few actions to reach a more solvable state, even when the goal remains distant. This reduces long-horizon learning to two coupled subproblems of reaching that state and completing the task from there. We address them with paired advantages and a progressive reverse-to-forward curriculum. The advantages provide separate signals for reaching more solvable states and completing the task from them, while the curriculum expands the capability region backward along successful reference trajectories and then into off-reference states through on-policy exploration. On ALFWorld and WebShop, our method outperforms competitive agentic RL methods at both model scales, achieving success rates of 90.1%/96.1% and 80.2%/82.6% with Qwen2.5-1.5B/7B-Instruct, respectively.

infographic.key_insight: A reverse-to-forward curriculum with paired advantage signals helps LLM agents learn long-horizon tasks by first mastering states closer to reliable success.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach offers a training strategy for tool-using agents facing sparse terminal rewards and difficult exploration.
method: Define a capability region: states from which the current policy can reliably complete the task.
Use paired advantages to separately reward reaching more solvable states and completing tasks from them.
Expand competence backward along successful reference trajectories, then into off-reference states through on-policy exploration.
infographic.evidence_signal: On ALFWorld and WebShop, the method outperforms competitive agentic RL baselines, reaching 90.1%/96.1% and 80.2%/82.6% success, respectively, with Qwen2.5-1.5B/7B-Instruct.
infographic.watch_item: The curriculum uses successful reference trajectories; their acquisition cost and the method's robustness to reference quality are not established in the abstract.
infographic.paper_title: Depth Before Breadth: Reverse-to-Forward Curriculum with Advantage Decomposition for LLM Agent

title: Local AI Agents in Power Electronics Simulation: Deployment, Measurements and Costs
authors: Yuzhuo Li, Pasan Gunawardena, Yunwei Li
abstract: Agentic artificial intelligence (AI) is emerging in power electronics, where it drives the simulation loop that engineers used to close largely by hand. In this loop, a converter design, or a study of the network it connects to, is built, run, measured and revised until it satisfies its specification. Such an agent can be served from a cloud API or from an inference device on the premises. For organizations whose designs, customer data or export-controlled material cannot leave the site, and whose simulators are licensed there, local deployment is the natural choice. In such a deployment, the agent becomes an electrical load on the organization's own equipment, i.e., every run consumes power and energy on a local device, generates tokens and takes time. However, existing work focuses mainly on what the agent can achieve with cloud-hosted models. What a local deployment costs in power, energy, tokens and time on real simulation tasks, and what its choices trade against one another, has received little quantitative investigation under comparable conditions. To address this gap, a systematic evaluation framework is presented in this paper. It applies locally served models to agentic power electronics tasks, from the converter level to the system level, and measures their power, energy, token and time costs. Based on these measurements, the capability boundary of a local agent on such tasks and the cost per solved task are characterized. The results are expected to provide practical insight for the use of agentic AI in power electronics and the power systems it serves.

infographic.key_insight: Local AI agents bring power-electronics simulation workflows on premises, making their capability and per-task power, energy, token and time costs important engineering considerations.
infographic.engineering_relevance: On-premises deployment supports workflows where sensitive designs must remain on site and simulators are locally licensed, but adds demand to local computing infrastructure.
method: Apply locally served models to agentic simulation tasks from converter to system level.
Measure power, energy, token use and elapsed time under comparable conditions.
Characterize capability boundaries and cost per solved task.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract describes a systematic measurement framework but reports no numerical results, model comparisons or task success rates.
infographic.watch_item: Practical performance and cost advantages remain unquantified in the abstract and require validation on the intended hardware and simulation workload.
infographic.paper_title: Local AI Agents in Power Electronics Simulation: Deployment, Measurements and Costs

title: Soft Mixture of Quantum Experts for Hybrid Quantum-Classical Learning
authors: Valeria Repetto, Romina D'Aurizio, Piero Farinelli
abstract: Quantum Machine Learning (QML) has attracted increasing interest as a possible route to construct feature representations that are difficult to reproduce with classical models. However, near-term QML architectures based on trainable parametrized quantum circuits remain affected by limited hardware resources, noise, and severe optimization difficulties such as barren plateaus. In this work we propose Soft-MoQE, a Soft Mixture of Quantum Experts architecture that replaces variational quantum training with the input-dependent selection and combination of fixed quantum feature maps. The model is composed of a heterogeneous pool of non-trainable quantum circuits, each defining a distinct embedding, and a classical gating network that learns how to weight these embeddings for each data point. We benchmark Soft-MoQE on three PCA-reduced tasks: MNIST parity, MNIST 10-class, and FashionMNIST. Soft-MoQE outperforms the single best expert, the uniform average of all experts and a linear baseline, achieving task-dependent performance comparable to that of a trainable quantum neural network, without optimizing any quantum parameter and with a quantum training cost that is lower by orders of magnitude. The analysis of the class- conditioned expert usage shows that the learned routing combines a few experts for each input, with a selection that depends on the class. These results support the learned routing among fixed quantum circuits as a trainability-aware design principle for hybrid QML.

infographic.key_insight: Soft-MoQE learns input-dependent combinations of fixed quantum feature maps, avoiding quantum parameter optimization while retaining competitive predictive performance.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Training only a classical gating network offers a resource-conscious approach to hybrid QML that sidesteps optimization difficulties associated with trainable quantum circuits.
method: Build a heterogeneous pool of fixed, non-trainable quantum circuits.
Train a classical gating network to weight each circuit's embedding for each input.
Combine quantum embeddings through learned soft routing.
infographic.evidence_signal: On PCA-reduced MNIST parity, MNIST 10-class, and FashionMNIST, Soft-MoQE outperforms the best single expert, uniform averaging, and a linear baseline, with task-dependent performance comparable to a trainable quantum neural network and orders-of-magnitude lower quantum training cost.
infographic.watch_item: Results are limited to PCA-reduced benchmarks; robustness to hardware noise and scaling to larger inputs remain unclear from the abstract.
infographic.paper_title: Soft Mixture of Quantum Experts for Hybrid Quantum-Classical Learning

title: A Foundation Model to Measure and Predict Human Behaviour
authors: Haoran Ye, Tianrui Huo, Hangzhen Li, Xin Zhang, Guojie Song
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used to infer psychological attributes, predict individual behaviour, and simulate human populations. However, despite generating plausible responses, they often misrepresent individuals and distort population statistics. Here we introduce Chiron, a foundation model to measure and predict human behaviour. We jointly fine-tune an LLM to represent psychological constructs, predict individual behaviour, and align population response distributions with human statistics. The training and evaluation data span 36 behavioural domains and 78 social science experiments, comprising 288,307 person records, 1,411,750 atomic behavioural decisions, and 99,953 psychometric assessments over 109 psychological constructs. In our evaluations, Chiron's psychological measurements agree more closely with human self-reports and exhibit fewer biases that undermine psychometric validity. It predicts individual behaviour more accurately than frontier LLMs (up to 28.4% relative improvement). In simulations of social science experiments, it more accurately captures the direction and magnitude of human experimental effects (82.2--94.3% lower effect-size estimation error). Together, these results establish Chiron as a unified computational instrument for measuring and predicting human behaviour.

infographic.key_insight: Chiron jointly learns psychological measurement, individual behaviour prediction, and population-level alignment to better represent human behaviour than general-purpose LLMs.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Chiron offers a unified approach for behavioural modelling and population simulation where plausible responses alone are insufficient.
method: Fine-tune an LLM to represent psychological constructs.
Jointly train individual behaviour prediction and population response-distribution alignment.
Evaluate psychological validity, prediction accuracy, and experimental effect-size estimates.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across 36 behavioural domains and 78 experiments, the dataset includes 288,307 person records, 1,411,750 decisions, and 99,953 psychometric assessments; evaluations report up to 28.4% relative prediction improvement over frontier LLMs and 82.2–94.3% lower effect-size estimation error.
infographic.watch_item: Generalisation to populations and behavioural settings beyond those evaluated remains unestablished in the abstract.
infographic.paper_title: A Foundation Model to Measure and Predict Human Behaviour

title: Synthesizing hyperspectral Data using generative Models to train spectral Unmixing Methods for low-cost Crop Residue Cover Mapping
authors: Ege Artan, Shuo Chen, Andrew Peng, Sammuel Aldrich Karya, Kyaw Thiha
abstract: The spectral range of the Field Imaging Nanosatellite for Crop residue Hyperspectral Mapping (FINCH), developed by the University of Toronto Aerospace Team's Space System Division, poses significant challenges for hyperspectral unmixing to determine crop residue cover fractional abundances. The severe lack of standard indices necessitates the use of complex, data-driven unmixing models. Complex unmixing models require dense, well-distributed manifolds, whereas ground-truth datasets are sparse and expensive. To better leverage the information content in existing ground-truth datasets, this study presents a framework that decouples interpolation and abundance-mapping estimation via an intermediary conditional data generator, contrasting with traditional single-model unmixing pipelines. This decoupling enables the inclusion of physical prior knowledge about spectra, which is not natively accessible to unmixing models, thereby artificially expanding the dataset to serve as a Monte Carlo approximation of the population risk. To test this hypothesis, we have proposed two generator models: a 1D Conditional U-Net with Conformer Layers (GD-Streamline) and a Dual-Path Transformer Conditional Variational AutoEncoder (TCVAE), and two unmixing models: Multi-Layered Perceptrons (MLP) and Fourier Neural Operators (FNO). The results of the study indicate a need for rigorous integration and introduction of spectral priors within the scope of the proposed decoupling framework to prevent domain and mode collapse and hallucination by the generator models; otherwise, this leads to falsely approximated data manifolds, ultimately resulting in unsatisfactory and out-of-distribution unmixing performance.

infographic.key_insight: Separating hyperspectral data generation from spectral unmixing offers a way to expand sparse training data, but unreliable synthetic spectra can undermine crop residue cover estimates.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Low-cost crop residue mapping with FINCH requires physically grounded training data because its spectral range limits standard index-based approaches.
method: Decouple conditional spectrum generation from abundance estimation.
Test GD-Streamline, a conditional U-Net with Conformer layers, and TCVAE, a dual-path Transformer conditional variational autoencoder.
Use generated data to train MLP and Fourier Neural Operator unmixing models.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract reports unsatisfactory and out-of-distribution unmixing performance associated with distorted synthetic data manifolds, without quantitative metrics or dataset sizes.
infographic.watch_item: Spectral priors need rigorous integration to prevent generator domain collapse, mode collapse, and hallucination.
infographic.paper_title: Synthesizing hyperspectral Data using generative Models to train spectral Unmixing Methods for low-cost Crop Residue Cover Mapping

title: GateWatch: Low-Overhead LLM Monitoring with Boolean Circuits
authors: Firas Spanioli, Yaniv David
abstract: As large language models (LLMs) and LLM-based agents are increasingly deployed, monitoring their behavior becomes important for detecting unsafe or unintended actions. Activation probes offer an efficient approach, but existing methods face trade-offs between accuracy, interpretability, and computational overhead. Probes on raw activations lack interpretable inputs, whereas sparse autoencoder (SAE) probes use interpretable features but often rely on additive classifiers and large SAE encoders, limiting interpretability and increasing memory overhead. We introduce GateWatch, a compact, interpretable classifier that expresses its entire decision rule as an explicit Boolean logic over a small number of binarized SAE features. We explore three approaches to constructing these circuits under a specified gate budget. For efficient deployment, GateWatchServe computes only selected SAE features, enables streaming of their binary values across layers during inference, and evaluates multiple GateWatch classifiers in parallel using compact lookup tables. Across 24 tasks on Gemma-2-9B, GateWatch achieves 80.49% mean test accuracy using only 3.8 SAE features and 3.5 logic gates per probe on average, just 1.17 percentage points below full 16K-feature SAE probes, while matching or outperforming them on 10 tasks and reducing probe memory by 99.98%. Inside vLLM, 1,000 concurrent multi-layer, multi-token GateWatch classifiers retain 97-98% of baseline throughput and 99.8% of KV-cache capacity.

infographic.key_insight: GateWatch turns a few binarized SAE features into explicit Boolean monitoring rules, approaching full SAE-probe accuracy with dramatically lower memory use.
infographic.engineering_relevance: GateWatchServe supports large numbers of concurrent LLM monitors with minimal inference-throughput and KV-cache impact.
method: Construct Boolean circuits over selected SAE features under a specified logic-gate budget.
Compute only selected features and stream their binary values across model layers.
Evaluate multiple classifiers in parallel using compact lookup tables.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across 24 tasks on Gemma-2-9B, GateWatch averaged 80.49% test accuracy with 3.8 features and 3.5 gates per probe—1.17 percentage points below full 16K-feature SAE probes—while reducing probe memory by 99.98%; 1,000 concurrent classifiers in vLLM retained 97–98% of baseline throughput and 99.8% of KV-cache capacity.
infographic.watch_item: Results are reported for Gemma-2-9B; accuracy and deployment overhead need validation on other models and monitoring tasks.
infographic.paper_title: GateWatch: Low-Overhead LLM Monitoring with Boolean Circuits

title: Surrogate Modeling and Reduced-Order Methods in Gravitational-Wave Physics and Numerical Relativity: From Spectral Representations to Adaptive Compression
authors: Manuel Tiglio
abstract: The rapid expansion of gravitational-wave astronomy and high-precision numerical relativity has created an acute computational bottleneck: direct numerical integration of the Einstein field equations and high-dimensional Bayesian parameter estimation require millions of waveform evaluations that cannot be sustained by traditional solvers alone. Reduced-order modeling (ROM) and surrogate techniques have emerged as foundational tools to bridge this gap, compressing high-fidelity solution manifolds into compact, rapidly evaluable representations without sacrificing physical accuracy. This perspective reviews the mathematical pillars of projection-based reduced-order modeling---including Proper Orthogonal Decomposition, greedy basis selection, and the Empirical Interpolation Method---and traces their operational impact in gravitational-wave data analysis through surrogate waveform families and Reduced-Order Quadratures. We then examine the fundamental approximation barriers posed by slow Kolmogorov n-width decay in non-stationary, transient, and strongly nonlinear regimes, showing how adaptive hp-greedy domain partitioning and multi-scale spectral compression overcome these limits. Finally, we discuss how combining certified reduced-order structures with modern scientific machine learning and sensitivity-aware quantization provides a rigorous blueprint for next-generation detectors such as LISA, Einstein Telescope, and Cosmic Explorer.

infographic.key_insight: Reduced-order models and waveform surrogates compress expensive gravitational-wave simulations into fast representations, while adaptive methods address regimes that resist global compression.
infographic.engineering_relevance: These methods can reduce waveform-generation and Bayesian-inference costs, supporting analysis pipelines for LISA, Einstein Telescope, and Cosmic Explorer.
method: Construct compact bases using Proper Orthogonal Decomposition or greedy selection, with empirical interpolation for rapid evaluation.
Use surrogate waveforms and Reduced-Order Quadratures to accelerate gravitational-wave inference.
Apply adaptive hp-greedy partitioning and multi-scale spectral compression to difficult solution regimes.
infographic.evidence_signal: The abstract presents a perspective reviewing mathematical foundations and operational applications, but reports no datasets, quantitative benchmarks, or measured speedups.
infographic.watch_item: Slow Kolmogorov n-width decay can limit global compression in transient or strongly nonlinear regimes, making adaptive partitioning and error validation important.
infographic.paper_title: Surrogate Modeling and Reduced-Order Methods in Gravitational-Wave Physics and Numerical Relativity: From Spectral Representations to Adaptive Compression

title: Piccolo: Co-Evolving Decision Models and Data through Recursive Self-Improvement
authors: Zhenqing Ling, Qirui Jiao, Daoyuan Chen, Cheng Chen, Xinji Mai, Haowen Gao
abstract: We present Piccolo, a family of multimodal decision models (0.8B to 27B) that coevolves model capabilities and training data via Agentic Data Engineering and recursive self-improvement (RSI). The models predict probabilities over candidate answers for general-purpose text and visual judgments, agent harnesses, data workflows, and interactive games. Piccolo-27B tops the Decision Index Vision Full leaderboard with a score of 75.59, while Piccolo-9B and Piccolo-4B achieve 68.35 and 67.46, respectively. All three rank first on the Private benchmark in their respective model-size categories. Research agents analyze model behavior, construct training data, conduct experiments, and use the results to refine subsequent proposals. Semantic slices and a shared research memory connect these actions across the model family's development. With training recipes comprising hundreds of thousands of examples, data selection and feedback-driven refinement are central to the self-improvement process. Our large-scale RSI exploration yields three counter-intuitive insights for decision-model development: (1) Backbone-recipe co-adaptation outweighs raw model recency: earlier backbones can surpass newer generations on visual tasks under identical recipes; (2) Targeted data curation enables 4B-9B models to rival 27B baselines on specialized workflows; and (3) Continuous loss reduction can decouple from and even degrade discrete decision accuracy. Together with the released weights and tools from the Data-Juicer and AgentScope ecosystems, Piccolo provides an actionable blueprint for building frontier decision models and scaling data-driven RSI.

infographic.key_insight: Piccolo co-evolves multimodal decision models and training data through recursive self-improvement, emphasizing targeted data curation over model scale alone.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The approach offers a blueprint for improving decision systems through feedback-driven data workflows and coordinated research agents.
method: Predict probabilities over candidate answers for text and visual decisions.
Use research agents to analyze behavior, curate training data, and run experiments.
Connect iterative improvements through semantic slices and shared research memory.
infographic.evidence_signal: On Decision Index Vision Full, Piccolo-27B scores 75.59, while 9B and 4B score 68.35 and 67.46; all three rank first on the Private benchmark within their respective size categories.
infographic.watch_item: Falling training loss can coincide with worse discrete decision accuracy, so refinement requires direct evaluation of task-level outcomes.
infographic.paper_title: Piccolo: Co-Evolving Decision Models and Data through Recursive Self-Improvement

title: Ground, Iterate, Trace: Decomposing AI Research Ideation
authors: Samson Yu, Qiran Zou, Jing Yu Lim, Rushi Shah, Anirudh Goyal, Dianbo Liu
abstract: Large language models have been widely used to generate plausible research ideas, yet it remains unclear what makes automated ideation effective and how generated novel proposals arise from prior scientific work. We introduce the Creative AI Researcher (CAR), an agentic framework combining literature grounding, iterative development and explicit conceptual operators. CAR constructs a semantic knowledge graph from retrieved literature and equips an ideation agent with graph-retrieval tools and four operators: bisociation, analogy, exploration and elaboration. Each operator call is checked against structural acceptance conditions and recorded, producing a trace of intermediate transformations and declared literature sources. We evaluate CAR with two language-model backbones across 40 LiveIdeaBench research topics and two execution benchmarks. CAR achieves significantly higher methodological novelty (MN) than single-shot prompting and The AI Scientist. Its methodological novelty does not differ significantly from the Research Ideation Agent, while its feasibility scores are higher on both backbones. With a shared experiment executor, CAR achieves the highest pairwise win rate among the evaluated AI methods on FML-bench-Lite and BioXArena. In a ten-condition ablation study, MN point estimates favor CAR over one-step proposal on both backbones, but no MN contrast survives correction for multiple comparisons. The results do not establish a consistent quality benefit from explicit operators beyond free-form iteration. CAR makes the sequence of operations and declared literature sources inspectable, separating judged idea quality from procedural traceability.

infographic.key_insight: CAR makes AI research ideation inspectable through literature-grounded transformation traces, while explicit operators show no consistent quality advantage over free-form iteration.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Research-agent pipelines can use knowledge-graph retrieval and logged conceptual transformations to inspect how proposals develop and which literature sources they declare.
method: Build a semantic knowledge graph from retrieved literature.
Iteratively develop ideas using graph retrieval and four operators: bisociation, analogy, exploration and elaboration.
Check operator calls against structural acceptance conditions and record transformations and declared sources.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across two model backbones, 40 LiveIdeaBench topics and two execution benchmarks, CAR outperformed single-shot prompting and The AI Scientist on methodological novelty and achieved the highest pairwise execution win rate among evaluated AI methods.
infographic.watch_item: No methodological-novelty contrast in the ten-condition ablation survived multiple-comparison correction, limiting claims about which components improve idea quality.
infographic.paper_title: Ground, Iterate, Trace: Decomposing AI Research Ideation

title: LLM-Guided Cyber-Physical Attack Path Identification in Smart Grids
authors: Amr Elshazly, Jesse Roberts, Rachad Atat, Muhammad Ismail
abstract: Identifying high-impact attack paths in cyber-physical power systems is critical for improving grid resilience. Existing methods typically rely on either structural topology analysis or simulation-based cascading-failure models. Topology-based approaches capture connectivity but lack adversarial reasoning, while simulation-driven methods are primarily suited for offline analysis and are less effective for rapid evaluation of evolving attack scenarios. As a result, identifying realistic attack paths that jointly capture topology, threat semantics, and physical impact remains challenging. This paper presents a physics-grounded framework for identifying cyber-physical attack paths using large language models (LLMs), with cascading-failure-derived impact rankings used as physics-grounded references. The framework integrates system topology, LLM-guided STRIDE and MITRE ATT&CK threat modeling, and three baseline strategies for comparison: topology-driven, threat-driven, and fusion-based. Evaluation is performed using (i) critical-node overlap between LLM-inferred top-K rankings and cascading-failure-based ground truth; (ii) node-level similarity between LLM-inferred and reference paths; and (iii) path-level alignment capturing agreement in complete attack sequences. Results show that structured LLM-based threat modeling substantially improves alignment with physics-grounded references. In the cyber layer, critical-node overlap@3 increases from approximately 33% to as high as 100%, while node-level similarity reaches up to 65% and path-level alignment reaches up to 48%. In addition, the proposed framework reduces runtime by approximately 75--85% compared to the fusion-based baseline in the IEEE 14-bus system. These results suggest that LLM-guided attack path identification is a promising approach for efficient and impact-aware cyber-physical security analysis.

infographic.key_insight: Structured LLM-guided threat modeling identifies smart-grid attack paths that better align with physics-grounded impact references while reducing analysis runtime.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework could help grid-security engineers prioritize high-impact cyber-physical attack scenarios for faster resilience assessment.
method: Combine system topology with LLM-guided STRIDE and MITRE ATT&CK threat modeling.
Use cascading-failure-derived impact rankings as physics-grounded references.
Compare against topology-driven, threat-driven, and fusion-based baselines.
infographic.evidence_signal: Reported cyber-layer critical-node overlap@3 rises from approximately 33% to as high as 100%, node-level similarity reaches 65%, and path-level alignment reaches 48%; runtime falls approximately 75–85% versus the fusion baseline on IEEE 14-bus.
infographic.watch_item: Generalization to larger operational grids remains unclear, and alignment with simulation-derived references does not establish real-world attack feasibility.
infographic.paper_title: LLM-Guided Cyber-Physical Attack Path Identification in Smart Grids

title: Meta-LSQ: A Closed-Form Sobolev Inner Solver for Few-Shot Meta-Learning
authors: Antonin Sulc
abstract: Gradient-based meta-learners such as model-agnostic meta-learning (MAML) adapt to a new task with an inner loop of gradient descent that has to be differentiated through, and they meta-learn every network weight. Meta-LSQ instead fits each task with one regularised least-squares solve over a fixed random Fourier basis and meta-learns only three scalars, a bandwidth, a ridge and a derivative weight. Since the derivative of a sinusoid is again a sinusoid, the same solve can also take derivative observations, and the fitted model has exact closed-form derivatives of any order. On 10-shot sinusoid regression Meta-LSQ trains in 14 s and ends with a 5.5 times lower error than a first-order MAML baseline that trains 36 times longer, and a Gaussian-process control suggests that most of this gain comes from sharing one kernel across tasks. In simulated beam tuning at DESY's ARES facility with model derivatives it is slightly more accurate than an ALPaCA-style model and well ahead of gradient descent. Over DESY's full range of target beams, again in simulation and from measurements alone, its best setting has a median error of 7.3 $μ$m, against 14.4 for the published final beams of their reinforcement-learning agent, which has the lower median on their 300 trials of small targets. On real sensor-calibration data a learned prior mean puts it ahead of MAML on two of four targets, but an exact Gaussian process with the same change and an ALPaCA-style model stay more accurate on most targets, and it breaks down on non-smooth targets. On noiseless targets outside the span of the basis, in-sample criteria such as generalised cross-validation choose too small a ridge.

infographic.key_insight: Meta-LSQ replaces gradient-based task adaptation with one regularised least-squares solve, meta-learning only bandwidth, ridge strength and derivative weight.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Fast adaptation and exact model derivatives make it promising for few-shot calibration and smooth engineering optimisation with scarce measurements.
method: Represent tasks using a fixed random Fourier basis.
Fit function values and optional derivative observations in one Sobolev least-squares solve.
Share three learned hyperparameters across tasks.
infographic.evidence_signal: On 10-shot sinusoid regression, Meta-LSQ trained in 14 seconds with 5.5× lower error than first-order MAML; simulated beam tuning and real sensor calibration showed task-dependent gains.
infographic.watch_item: Performance breaks down on non-smooth targets, and in-sample ridge selection can under-regularise noiseless targets outside the basis span.
infographic.paper_title: Meta-LSQ: A Closed-Form Sobolev Inner Solver for Few-Shot Meta-Learning

title: Openhagen Worlds: Calibrated Environments for Measuring and Training Scientific Discovery Agents
authors: Alexander Boesgaard Lorup
abstract: Agents that do science must choose informative experiments and reason from their results, but most discovery benchmarks cannot separate that skill from recall, unstated scoring rules or shortcut policies. We introduce Openhagen Worlds, a suite of 27 procedurally generated environments (some with finite truth spaces), from classic puzzles of experimental reasoning to simulator-grounded physics and chemistry, in which an agent runs experiments under a budget and commits an answer that a deterministic verifier checks against a hidden truth. Every observation states the complete scoring rule, and each of the 178 difficulty levels is calibrated: it is admitted only if, on 64 development instances, a scripted oracle succeeds on at least 0.75, the strongest plausible non-deductive policy on at most 0.25 and each gated shortcut on at most 0.35. The 92 core levels span all 27 families and are sized to train small models; the 86 frontier rungs extend the 15 discovery worlds with harder questions and with campaigns of three, five and eight or more committed stages on one hidden system. On the same 84 withheld frontier instances, one per family and rung, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash solves 32 at its default reasoning effort with 16,384 tokens per call and 57 at its maximum effort with up to 393,216 tokens per call (oracle: 79); the headroom that remains is largest in eight-stage campaigns. On-policy expert iteration gives a 9B model modest gains: its core-tier success on trained families rises from 0.090 to 0.148, partly through better action format, with no detectable loss on GPQA Diamond. A hosted service plays the core tier's withheld instances.

infographic.key_insight: Openhagen Worlds measures experimental reasoning through 27 generated environments with explicit scoring rules, hidden truths and calibrated difficulty.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The suite provides budgeted, automatically verified tasks for training and evaluating agents that choose experiments and infer scientific answers.
method: Agents run experiments under a budget, then commit answers checked by deterministic verifiers.
Calibrate 178 levels on 64 development instances each, requiring high oracle success and low non-deductive and shortcut success.
Split tasks into 92 core levels for smaller models and 86 frontier levels featuring harder questions and multistage campaigns.
infographic.evidence_signal: On 84 withheld frontier instances, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash solved 32 at default reasoning effort and 57 at maximum effort, versus 79 for the oracle.
infographic.watch_item: Calibration tests specified baseline and shortcut policies, so it does not establish resistance to every possible shortcut.
infographic.paper_title: Openhagen Worlds: Calibrated Environments for Measuring and Training Scientific Discovery Agents

title: Decomposing SGD Dynamics in Neural Networks: Teacher-Induced Spikes and Variance Inflation
authors: Samet Demir, Zafer Dogan
abstract: We study two-layer neural networks trained by stochastic gradient descent (SGD) on a multi-index teacher model, focusing on how first-layer parameters orthogonal to the teacher subspace affect generalization. We decompose the first-layer weights into a signal component aligned with the teacher and an orthogonal complement, and analyze their joint SGD dynamics together with the second layer in the proportional limit. We show that although SGD updates to the complement are initially isotropic, the training dynamics induce teacher-dependent spectral spikes in the complement Gram matrix. This emergent anisotropy provides a concrete mechanism by which representation variance is amplified, and generalization degrades. To isolate this effect, we introduce Decomposed Dynamics, an analytically tractable surrogate whose asymptotic test-error dynamics coincide with those of SGD. In simulations with a ReLU student, freezing the directions of the orthogonal complement improves generalization relative to training them. Finally, we show that the signal component rapidly aligns with the second-layer weights, revealing strong cross-layer coupling even in this shallow setting. Together, our results provide a dynamical explanation for how feature learning outside the teacher subspace harms generalization.

infographic.key_insight: SGD induces teacher-dependent spectral spikes outside the teacher subspace, amplifying representation variance and degrading generalization.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Controlling feature updates outside task-relevant directions may improve generalization in neural networks.
method: Decompose first-layer weights into teacher-aligned and orthogonal components.
Analyze joint SGD dynamics with the second layer in the proportional limit.
Introduce Decomposed Dynamics, a tractable surrogate matching SGD’s asymptotic test-error dynamics.
infographic.evidence_signal: ReLU-student simulations show better generalization when orthogonal-complement directions are frozen rather than trained.
infographic.watch_item: The analysis concerns two-layer networks and a multi-index teacher model; applicability to deeper networks and real-world data remains unestablished.
infographic.paper_title: Decomposing SGD Dynamics in Neural Networks: Teacher-Induced Spikes and Variance Inflation

title: Cap-and-Track: Optimizing LLM Inference Request Dispatch Across Shifting Capacity
authors: Benjamin Novotny, Doug Szeto, Chang Wang, Shicheng Chen, George Zhihua Yuan, Bob Kamma
abstract: A fixed dispatch rate for LLM inference becomes stale as serving fleets resize and request sizes change. Generative output length is unknown at admission, and shared provider pools can lose capacity. We present Cap-and-Track, a design for asynchronous inference across provider capacity and internal GPUs. Meta's traffic shaper implements Cap-and-Track for post and live-video understanding. Refusals signal the backend's current admission ceiling. Durable priority queues hold excess work outside execution, including refused requests for retry. Cap is a fail-fast admission check at the saturated resource that refuses work before a long wait. Using only those refusals, the Track dispatcher probes upward and backs off. It follows the ceiling without output-length prediction or a fleet-level rate to retune. In a concurrent same-traffic production A/B, the shaper ran per-replica Cap plus Track. It served a classifier on 43% fewer H100s than its queued, fixed-rate precursor, though lower-priority work waited longer at backfill peaks. In steady-capacity real-engine replay, Track ran within 1% of the goodput of a fixed rate tuned above measured capacity, with about a quarter of that rate's refusal share. The shaper carries more than 300 million online requests and hundreds of terabytes of media a day. During a backfill, it handled 1.1 billion requests in its busiest 24 hours. Lessons include keeping queues inside inference engines just long enough to fill batches, steering dispatch by capacity refusals alone, keeping dispatch stateful, and sizing fleets by how long low-priority work can wait.

infographic.key_insight: Cap-and-Track adapts LLM inference dispatch to shifting capacity using admission refusals, without predicting output length or retuning a fleet-wide rate.
infographic.engineering_relevance: Separating durable waiting queues from inference execution can reduce GPU requirements while adapting to changing workloads and backend capacity.
method: Cap refuses requests at the saturated resource before long execution-side waits form.
Track probes upward and backs off using capacity refusals alone.
Durable priority queues hold excess and refused requests for later dispatch.
infographic.evidence_signal: A concurrent production A/B served a classifier on 43% fewer H100s than the queued, fixed-rate precursor; steady-capacity real-engine replay achieved goodput within 1% of an above-capacity fixed rate with about one-quarter of its refusal share.
infographic.watch_item: Lower-priority work waited longer during backfill peaks, so fleet sizing must account for acceptable queueing delays.
infographic.paper_title: Cap-and-Track: Optimizing LLM Inference Request Dispatch Across Shifting Capacity

title: Choosing the Right Representations: Task-Aware Fusion for Multimodal Materials Language Models
authors: Huu Binh Ta, Alex Morehead, N. Benjamin Erichson, Ferdinando Fioretto, Sandeep Madireddy
abstract: Multimodal language models for materials science rely on effective mechanisms for incorporating three-dimensional structural representations. MatterChat addresses this challenge using a large bridge module between a pretrained structural encoder and the LLM, together with a separate contrastive alignment stage. We instead ask whether this bridge can adaptively select and combine representations from multiple structural encoders according to the target property. We find that supervised and generative material encoders provide complementary information for property prediction. We found that, for Zatom-1, this information is not concentrated in the final layer. Instead, the most informative representations occur at different depths depending on the target property. This motivates Task-Conditioned Attention Fusion (TCAF), a lightweight attention-based bridge that uses task-conditioned latent queries to combine CHGNet features with intermediate Zatom-1 representations. The bridge is trained directly on downstream prediction tasks, allowing representation selection and material-language alignment to be learned jointly without separate contrastive pretraining. Across classification and regression tasks, TCAF outperforms MatterChat, with up to 47.8% lower RMSE, while using substantially fewer trainable parameters and halving the overall training time. Further experiments incorporating UMA-S demonstrate TCAF's flexibility across encoder combinations, with the three-encoder configuration achieving the highest macro-average classification accuracy of 89.61%.

infographic.key_insight: Task-aware fusion of complementary structural encoders and intermediate layers improves materials-property prediction over a fixed representation bridge.
infographic.engineering_relevance: TCAF offers a more parameter-efficient bridge for materials language models, with reported gains in prediction quality and roughly half the overall training time of MatterChat.
method: Combine CHGNet features with intermediate Zatom-1 representations.
Use task-conditioned latent queries to select and fuse representations through attention.
Train the bridge directly on downstream prediction tasks without separate contrastive pretraining.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across classification and regression tasks, TCAF outperforms MatterChat with up to 47.8% lower RMSE; adding UMA-S yields the highest macro-average classification accuracy of 89.61%.
infographic.watch_item: The abstract does not specify dataset sizes or out-of-distribution tests, leaving generalization to unfamiliar materials uncertain.
infographic.paper_title: Choosing the Right Representations: Task-Aware Fusion for Multimodal Materials Language Models

title: A Generative Model for Higher-Order Network Dynamics
authors: Valentina Sánchez, Theodore Papamarkou, Gonzalo Nápoles, Çiçek Güven, Koen V. Haak
abstract: Conventional network representations inferred from multivariate time series describe statistical relationships between pairs of components, even when the underlying dynamics involve group interactions that cannot be represented by pairwise interactions alone. Several multivariate information-theoretic measures have been proposed to characterise dependence beyond pairs. However, due to a lack of systems with known generating mechanisms, these measures have not been carefully validated or compared for empirical use. To address this, we here introduce a generative model of stochastic network dynamics with pairwise and higher-order interactions specified by the user. The higher-order interactions are represented by directed hyperedges, and the model provides a controlled benchmark for evaluating information-theoretic measures. Removing only the higher-order term gives a pairwise-only reference. The experiments test whether a measure detects changes induced by the higher-order term relative to this reference and recovers the participating nodes and their source-target roles. A separate experiment tests discrimination between a product coupling and a specified nonlinear pairwise control, with equal root-mean-square coupling magnitude under the pairwise-only reference. Several measures detected sufficiently strong higher-order interactions across the tested network topologies and coupling functions. In the separate discrimination experiment, the measures also separated the product coupling from the specified nonlinear pairwise control. Recovery, however, became harder as the number of candidate interactions grew. The framework therefore provides a testbed where the link between higher-order signatures and mechanisms can be tested, rather than assumed, before measures are applied to empirical data.

infographic.key_insight: A stochastic network generator with user-defined directed hyperedges enables controlled tests of whether information-theoretic measures identify higher-order interactions and their source–target roles.
infographic.engineering_relevance: The framework helps validate higher-order network analysis methods against known mechanisms before applying them to empirical multivariate time series.
method: Specify pairwise and higher-order couplings in stochastic network dynamics.
Remove the higher-order term to create a pairwise-only reference for detection and recovery tests.
Compare product coupling with a specified nonlinear pairwise control matched in RMS coupling magnitude under the reference.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across tested topologies and coupling functions, several measures detected sufficiently strong higher-order interactions and, in a separate experiment, distinguished product coupling from the specified nonlinear pairwise control.
infographic.watch_item: Recovery became harder as candidate interactions increased, so detection alone should not be treated as reliable identification of the underlying mechanism.
infographic.paper_title: A Generative Model for Higher-Order Network Dynamics
